deferred_source_units.reason: The general for-the-end and Davidic song heading has no distinctive named occasion or other sufficiently specific correspondence established here; shared authorship alone is not credited.

The Lord making His holy one wondrous and hearing the speaker's cry is read in context, but the holy one's identity is not supplied beyond this wording and no distinct target identification is established.
The heading concerning her who inherits leaves its feminine referent unnamed. An identification with a particular woman, congregation or later community would exceed the supplied title.
The request to hear words and understand the cry is part of the opening petition, but a further link based only on a general request to hear prayer would add no sufficiently particular comparison.
The address my King and my God and attention to petition is read, but a shared divine title and generic prayer address alone do not establish an additional retained relationship.

The line crowns the worshippers as with a weapon of favor. A familiar rendering about surrounding someone with a shield is not substituted, and no adequately specific comparison for the actual crowning-and-weapon formulation is established.

The request for return, rescue and salvation for mercy's sake is read with the bodily lament, but no additional sufficiently particular target beyond a general rescue petition is established for this unit.
The declaration that God heard and accepted the petition completes the lament's turn toward confidence. Generic answered-prayer counterparts are not added merely to credit the repeated assurance.
The wish for enemies' shame, disturbance and quick retreat is read as the lament's conclusion; no particular enemy event or sufficiently distinct additional counterpart is established.

The title names Chousi son of Iemeni. The separately read Hushai the Archite account does not establish this person's identity; the different supplied names and identifying descriptions remain unresolved.

The proposed Saul narrative shares a general plea for rescue from pursuit, but this unit does not identify Saul or supply an additional sufficiently distinctive correspondence. The comparison was removed after the complete-triple reread; the source remains pending.

The pursuit, trampling and dust form the consequence of the preceding conditional innocence oath. This full consequence was read as necessary context, but no separate particular counterpart is established merely from its grammatical continuation of that oath.

The assembly of peoples surrounding God and the request that He return on high remain in the judgment appeal. An identification with a particular heavenly ascent or named assembly is not established by the supplied words.
God's help for the upright in heart is read as part of the appeal to the just judge; a further connection based only on the broad assurance of help to the righteous would be too general.

Thanksgiving according to the Lord's righteousness and praise of the Most High conclude the psalm. Shared praise vocabulary or the divine title alone is not treated as an additional particular relationship.
The heading concerning the hidden things of the son does not identify the son or explain the hidden things. Neither a historical child nor a christological referent is assumed from this title alone.
The promise to rejoice, exult and praise the Most High is read, but repeated general praise language or the divine title alone does not establish a sufficiently particular additional target.

God's vindication of the speaker's case and righteous enthronement are read in context. No particular legal dispute is identified, and another generic judgment comparison is not added to the distinct throne-for-judgment link retained at 9:8.

The failed enemy swords, demolished cities and vanished memory have no identified historical event in this psalm. A generic destroyed-city narrative would not establish the particular connection needed here.
The assurance that God has not abandoned those seeking Him and the call for name-knowers to hope are read, but no further distinct connection beyond generalized trust and nonabandonment is retained.

The request is to appoint a lawgiver so that nations know they are human. A familiar alternative rendering about terror is not substituted, and no particular lawgiver or matching episode is established.

The supplied line says the poor man is set ablaze as the ungodly exalts himself and describes entrapment in devised counsels. Its pronouns and burning image are not replaced with another edition's pursuit wording or forced into a named oppression event.

The sinner's ways are said to be profaned, with divine judgments removed from before him and dominance over enemies. A prosperity rendering or a specific historical ruler is not imported to manufacture a connection.

The trap, humbling, bowing and falling amid domination of the needy have potentially shifting pronouns. No target is retained by silently deciding which action belongs to oppressor or victim beyond what the source establishes.

The call for God to arise, raise His hand and remember the needy is read within the larger rebuttal of divine inattention. Another general arise-or-remember petition is not retained without an additional particular correspondence.

The hearing of the needy desire and attention to the heart's preparation are read as the prayer's answer. No sufficiently distinct target beyond generic hearing of prayer is established for this formulation.

The title and running text together describe trust and advice to flee to the mountains like a little bird. The separately read Saul pursuit account contains a different night-raven comparison and does not establish this psalm's historical occasion.

The text says opponents pulled down what God established and asks what the righteous person did. It does not explicitly name foundations, so that familiar formulation is not used to create an unsupported comparison.

The supplied declaration says the Lord loves righteous deeds and His face beheld uprightness. It is not rewritten as the upright seeing God's face, and no sufficiently particular additional counterpart is established for the actual formulation.

unresolved_candidates.rationale: Psalm 6 says concerning the eighth, while the musicians in Chronicles play lyres, Amasenith. The supplied Chronicles unit does not translate that term as eighth, and the Psalm heading does not name those musicians or instruments. The proposed technical identity remains unresolved.

The Psalm title names Chousi son of Iemeni; the narrative identifies Hushai the Archite as David's companion. Association with David and a proposed name correspondence do not resolve the differing identifying descriptions or connect the Psalm to this narrated meeting.

The Psalm combines a Davidic title with advice to move to the mountains like a little bird. In the Saul narrative David says the king seeks his soul as the night-raven pursues in the mountains. The bird's role differs, and the shared mountain setting does not establish that the Psalm describes this episode.
